bmt-2021-general-01.title: Set up one equation
bmt-2021-general-01.body:
If Carson's school has $C$ students, Emily's has $4C$, so $5C=10105$ and $C=2021$.

**Answer: 2021**

bmt-2021-general-03.title: Make the other two angles as large as possible
bmt-2021-general-03.body:
To make one angle small, the other two must be large. Since the triangle is acute, each angle is at most $89^\circ$, and since it is scalene, the angles are distinct, so the two largest are at most $89^\circ$ and $88^\circ$. The third angle is then $180-89-88=3^\circ$ (and $3,88,89$ is a valid scalene acute triangle).

**Answer: 3**

bmt-2021-general-04.title: Rates
bmt-2021-general-04.body:
Moor drinks $\frac74$ cups per hour. From 8:00 to 11:15 he drinks for $3.25$ hours, and Samantha drinks from 10:00 to 11:15, i.e. $1.25$ hours. With Samantha's rate $s$: $3.25\cdot\frac74+1.25s=7$, so $1.25s=7-5.6875=1.3125$ and $s=1.05=\frac{21}{20}$ cups per hour. One cup takes her $\frac{20}{21}$ hour.

**Answer: $\frac{20}{21}$ hours**

bmt-2021-general-05.title: Two directions of cut
bmt-2021-general-05.body:
A cut parallel to a side of length $28$ gives boards $28\times a$ and $28\times(30-a)$; the cuts at $a$ and $30-a$ give the same pair, so $a=1,\dots,15$ gives $15$ pairs. A cut parallel to a side of length $30$ gives $30\times b$ and $30\times(28-b)$, so $b=1,\dots,14$ gives $14$ pairs. No pair arises in both ways (one board would have to have both a side of $28$ and a side of $30$ equal to something else), so the total is $15+14=29$.

**Answer: 29**

bmt-2021-general-06.title: Add the four surfaces
bmt-2021-general-06.body:
Two annular bases: $2\pi(8^2-2^2)=120\pi$. Outer lateral surface: $2\pi\cdot8\cdot6=96\pi$. Inner lateral surface: $2\pi\cdot2\cdot6=24\pi$. Total $240\pi$.

**Answer: $240\pi$**

bmt-2021-general-08.title: Find the totals
bmt-2021-general-08.body:
The yellow sector on day one is $360-210-60=90^\circ$, i.e. $\frac14$ of the students, so $165\cdot4=660$ students were polled. After day two there are $690$ students, still $165$ choosing yellow, so the new angle is $\frac{165}{690}\cdot360=\frac{1980}{23}^\circ$. The difference is $90-\frac{1980}{23}=\frac{90}{23}$ degrees.

**Answer: $\frac{90}{23}$**

bmt-2021-general-09.title: Only the first three flips matter
bmt-2021-general-09.body:
If the first three flips are not $HHH$, then a $T$ appears before the first $HHH$ could be completed, and after that $T$ the next time two heads come in a row, $THH$ has occurred first. More precisely, any $HHH$ not at the very start is preceded by a $T$ followed by $HH$, giving $THH$ first. So $HHH$ wins only if the first three flips are $HHH$: probability $\frac18$.

**Answer: $\frac18$**

bmt-2021-general-10.title: Similar triangles
bmt-2021-general-10.body:
Since $AB=AC$, $\angle ABC=\angle ACB$. Triangles $BCD$, $BAC$ and $CBE$ are similar (they share base angles and $\angle BCD=\angle BAC$), so $\frac{BD}{BC}=\frac{BC}{BA}=\frac23$ and $BD=12$; by symmetry (the triangles $BCD$ and $CBE$ are congruent) $CE=12$. Then $AD=AE=15$, so $DE\parallel BC$ and $DE=BC\cdot\frac{AD}{AB}=18\cdot\frac59=10$.

**Answer: 10**

bmt-2021-general-11.title: Complementary counting
bmt-2021-general-11.body:
There are $5^5=3125$ sequences. The gcd is greater than $1$ exactly when it is divisible by $2$, $3$ or $5$. All terms even (from $\{2,4\}$): $2^5=32$; all terms divisible by $3$ (only $3$): $1$; all divisible by $5$ (only $5$): $1$. These cases do not overlap (a sequence divisible by two of the primes would need terms $\ge6$ or $0$). So the answer is $3125-32-1-1=3091$.

**Answer: 3091**

bmt-2021-general-12.title: Vieta
bmt-2021-general-12.body:
$\frac1a+\frac1b+\frac1c=\frac{ab+bc+ca}{abc}$. By Vieta, $ab+bc+ca=-3\cdot2021^2$ and $abc=2\cdot2021^3$. The ratio is $-\frac{3}{2\cdot2021}=-\frac3{4042}$.

**Answer: $-\frac{3}{4042}$**

bmt-2021-general-13.title: Minimum at least 4 minus minimum at least 5
bmt-2021-general-13.body:
The minimum is at least $4$ with probability $\left(\frac36\right)^4$ and at least $5$ with probability $\left(\frac26\right)^4$. So the minimum equals $4$ with probability $\frac{3^4-2^4}{6^4}=\frac{65}{1296}$.

**Answer: $\frac{65}{1296}$**

bmt-2021-general-14.title: Roots of unity sum
bmt-2021-general-14.body:
Since $2020=47\cdot42+46$, $r_i^{2020}=r_i^{46}$. The map $r\mapsto r^{46}=r^{-1}$ permutes the $47$th roots of unity, so the sum equals the sum of all $47$th roots of unity, which is $0$ (the coefficient of $x^{46}$ in $x^{47}-1$).

**Answer: 0**

bmt-2021-general-15.title: Three chips never loop; four may
bmt-2021-general-15.body:
With at most three chips the firing always stops. When a fourth chip is added to a board of three chips on different squares, it lands on an occupied square with probability $\frac34$ and then an infinite loop of chip-fires occurs; with probability $\frac14$ it lands on the single empty square, and then any fifth chip lands on an occupied square and causes the loop. So the expected number of chips is $4\cdot\frac34+5\cdot\frac14=\frac{17}{4}$.

(A computer simulation of all chip-firing sequences, with squares adjacent when they share an edge, also gives $\frac{17}4$.)

**Answer: $\frac{17}{4}$**

bmt-2021-general-16.title: Area in the unit square
bmt-2021-general-16.body:
Let Jason's and Valerie's arrival times (in hours) be $x$ and $y$ in $[0,1]$. They fail to meet if $y-x>\frac13$ (Jason first and leaves) or $x-y>\frac16$ (Valerie first and leaves). The areas are $\frac12\left(\frac23\right)^2=\frac29$ and $\frac12\left(\frac56\right)^2=\frac{25}{72}$. So the probability of meeting is $1-\frac{16}{72}-\frac{25}{72}=\frac{31}{72}$.

**Answer: $\frac{31}{72}$**

bmt-2021-general-17.title: Denest the radicals
bmt-2021-general-17.body:
$17\pm12\sqrt2=(3\pm2\sqrt2)^2$, so the fourth roots are $\sqrt{3\pm2\sqrt2}$. And $3\pm2\sqrt2=(\sqrt2\pm1)^2$, so $\sqrt{3+2\sqrt2}=\sqrt2+1$ and $\sqrt{3-2\sqrt2}=\sqrt2-1$. The difference is $(\sqrt2+1)-(\sqrt2-1)=2$.

**Answer: 2**

bmt-2021-general-18.title: Reflect across $CD$
bmt-2021-general-18.body:
Since $BC\parallel AD$ (both perpendicular to $CD$), $\angle BAD=180^\circ-120^\circ=60^\circ$. So $CD=6\sin60^\circ=3\sqrt3$ and $AD-BC=6\cos60^\circ=3$, giving $BC=4$.

The condition $\angle AED=\angle BEC$ means $E$ is where the path $A\to E\to B$ reflects off line $CD$. Reflect $B$ over $CD$ to $B'$; then $AE+EB=AB'$. With $C=(0,0)$, $D=(0,3\sqrt3)$, $B=(4,0)$, $A=(7,3\sqrt3)$ we get $B'=(-4,0)$ and $AB'=\sqrt{11^2+(3\sqrt3)^2}=\sqrt{148}=2\sqrt{37}$.

**Answer: $2\sqrt{37}$**

bmt-2021-general-20.title: Geometric series
bmt-2021-general-20.body:
The sum is $(1+i)\frac{(1+i)^n-1}{(1+i)-1}=\frac{1+i}{i}\left((1+i)^n-1\right)=(1-i)\left((1+i)^n-1\right)$. Setting this equal to $(n^2-1)(1-i)$ gives $(1+i)^n=n^2$. This must be real, so $4\mid n$; write $n=4k$. Then $(1+i)^4=-4$ gives $(-4)^k=16k^2$. Trying $k=1,2,3$ fails, $k=4$ works ($256=256$), and for $k\ge5$ the exponential $4^k$ outgrows $16k^2$. So $n=16$.

**Answer: 16**

bmt-2021-general-21.title: Frobenius mod 13
bmt-2021-general-21.body:
Modulo $13$, $\left(1+\sqrt2\right)^{13}\equiv1+\left(\sqrt2\right)^{13}=1+2^6\sqrt2\equiv1-\sqrt2$, since $2^6\equiv-1\pmod{13}$. Also $(a+b\sqrt2)(1+\sqrt2)=\left(1+\sqrt2\right)^{13}$, i.e. $(a+2b)+(a+b)\sqrt2\equiv1-\sqrt2$. So $a+2b\equiv1$, $a+b\equiv-1$, giving $b\equiv2$, $a\equiv-3$ and $ab\equiv-6\equiv7$.

**Answer: 7**

bmt-2021-general-21.title: Direct computation
bmt-2021-general-21.body:
Multiplying by $1+\sqrt2$ twelve times (or squaring repeatedly) gives $(1+\sqrt2)^{12}=19601+13860\sqrt2$. Modulo $13$: $19601=13\cdot1507+10$ and $13860=13\cdot1066+2$, so $ab\equiv10\cdot2=20\equiv7$.

**Answer: 7**

bmt-2021-general-22.title: Count closed walks
bmt-2021-general-22.body:
The number of flight sequences of length $5$ from Lincoln back to Lincoln (each flight to a different city) is the number of closed walks of length $5$ in the complete graph $K_5$: $\frac{4^5+4\cdot(-1)^5}{5}=204$. The favorable sequences visit the other four cities in some order and then return to Lincoln: $4!=24$. The probability is $\frac{24}{204}=\frac2{17}$.

(Equivalently: $\frac{24/4^5}{51/256}=\frac2{17}$ using the probability $\frac{51}{256}$ of being back in Lincoln after five random flights.)

**Answer: $\frac{2}{17}$**

bmt-2021-general-23.title: Orientation argument
bmt-2021-general-23.body:
Reflections reverse the orientation of the labeling $ABCD$ and rotations preserve it. The last three moves are rotations or do-nothings, so the first three must together produce a rotation: an even number of reflections. Either all three are do-nothings ($1$ way), or exactly two are reflections and one is a do-nothing ($3\cdot4\cdot4=48$ ways), for $49$ ways in total.

The first three moves leave the square in one of the $4$ rotated positions. For the last three moves (each one of four rotation-type moves: none, $90^\circ$, $180^\circ$, $270^\circ$), the first two are free ($16$ ways) and the third is then forced to return to the start. Total $49\cdot16=784$ (confirmed by enumerating all sequences by computer).

**Answer: 784**

bmt-2021-general-24.title: Bound the smallest variable
bmt-2021-general-24.body:
Assume $z=\min(x,y,z)$. If $z\ge3$: $x=y=z=3$ already gives $27>18$, and increasing any variable by $1$ raises $xyz$ by at least $9$ but $2(x+y+z)$ only by $2$, so $xyz>2(x+y+z)$ whenever all are $\ge3$. So $z\in\{1,2\}$.

- $z=1$: $xy=2x+2y+2\Rightarrow(x-2)(y-2)=6$, giving $(x,y)=(8,3),(5,4)$ (and permutations): sums $12$ and $10$.
- $z=2$: $2xy=2x+2y+4\Rightarrow(x-1)(y-1)=3$, giving $(x,y)=(4,2)$ and $(2,4)$: sum $8$.

The possible values of $x+y+z$ are $8,10,12$, with total $30$.

**Answer: 30**

bmt-2021-general-25.title: Official approach (BO_n treated as a median)
bmt-2021-general-25.body:
The official solution takes $\overline{BO_n}$ and $\overline{TO_n}$ to be medians of $\triangle B_nMT_n$, so $B_{n+1},T_{n+1}$ are midpoints of $MB_n,MT_n$ and each triangle is half the previous one. Then $O_{n}$ is at height $1-\frac{2}{3\cdot2^n}$ above $BT$ and $[MBO_nT]=\frac12-\frac12\left(1-\frac2{3\cdot2^n}\right)=\frac1{3\cdot2^n}$, which would give $\frac1{3\cdot2^{2021}}$.

**Official answer: $\dfrac{1}{3\cdot2^{2021}}$**

bmt-2021-general-25.title: Literal reading with vectors
bmt-2021-general-25.body:
Put $M$ at the origin with $B=\mathbf b$, $T=\mathbf t$, so $[MBT]=\frac12$. Write $B_n=\beta_n\mathbf t$ on $MT$ and $T_n=\tau_n\mathbf b$ on $MB$ (with $\beta_0=\tau_0=1$ standing for the original $T$ and $B$). Then $O_n=\frac13(\beta_n\mathbf t+\tau_n\mathbf b)$. The line from $B=\mathbf b$ through $O_n$ is $\mathbf b+\lambda(O_n-\mathbf b)$; it meets $MT$ when the $\mathbf b$-coefficient $1-\lambda+\lambda\tau_n/3$ vanishes, i.e. $\lambda=\frac{3}{3-\tau_n}$, giving $\beta_{n+1}=\frac{\beta_n}{3-\tau_n}$ and symmetrically $\tau_{n+1}=\frac{\tau_n}{3-\beta_n}$. By symmetry $\beta_n=\tau_n=x_n$ with $x_{n+1}=\frac{x_n}{3-x_n}$, $x_0=1$. For $y_n=1/x_n$: $y_{n+1}=3y_n-1$, so $y_n=\frac{3^n+1}{2}$ and $x_n=\frac2{3^n+1}$.

The quadrilateral splits into triangles $MBO_n$ and $MO_nT$, each of area $\frac{x_n}{3}\cdot[MBT]=\frac{x_n}{6}$. So $[MBO_nT]=\frac{x_n}3=\frac{2}{3(3^n+1)}$, i.e. $\frac{2}{3(3^{2021}+1)}$ for $n=2021$.

**Answer (literal reading): $\dfrac{2}{3\left(3^{2021}+1\right)}$; the official key is $\dfrac{1}{3\cdot2^{2021}}$**
